title: Your agent architecture has a half-life of 6 months — Dan Farrelly, CTO, Inngest

summary: Dan Farrelly frames the problem: anyone building agents for more than six months has likely rewritten their architecture, because new models, frameworks, standards, and patterns constantly emerge. Rather than predicting the next trend, he advocates building a stable foundation that survives change. He identifies three discrete conceptual layers in agent systems. The execution layer (the brain) handles flow, state, durability, and retries. The context layer (knowledge) encompasses models, prompts, tools, and memory—the layer that changes most frequently. The compute layer (the hands) includes sandboxes, runtimes, and browsers. Each layer has a different half-life: prompts last weeks, models last months, but execution can last years if designed correctly. The core problem is that most teams couple these layers together, causing one layer's short half-life to drag down the others, creating technical debt. His thesis: think in layers and decouple them. The execution layer should manage the full lifecycle—plan, call models, run code, invoke sub-agents, loop, retry, coordinate—while remaining independent of the specific model, context, or sandbox used. Key execution requirements include resumability (picking up after failures without restarting, requiring durable and external state), flexible invocation patterns (crons, events, APIs, human-in-the-loop, subagents, synchronous and asynchronous execution), and full-session observability across triggers, LLM calls, tool calls, database errors, and performance. Sandboxes are ephemeral and stateless by design; using them for durability or state is an anti-pattern—the execution layer should give the sandbox its context and sequence. Farrelly previews upcoming architectures—background agents, dynamic workflows, autonomous loops, agent factories—all long-running, asynchronous, and delegated. He gives a complete example built from three functions: a cron-based health check that runs every 30 minutes, a triage agent that investigates root causes and spins up sandboxes, and a reviewer function that runs weekly to evaluate whether the triage system is working, whether prompts need adjustment, and whether the system has the data it needs. The reviewer must be execution-aware and orchestration-aware, pulling logs to understand what was executed, what sub-agents were fanned out, and what workflows were called. The execution layer sits between user input and system activity, making it an ideal hub for observability and scoring. By deferring scoring tasks after execution with full trace information, teams can create outcome-based scores—did the triage result in an opened PR? Was research saved?—rather than relying on simple thumbs-up feedback. He positions Inngest as the execution layer that provides durable steps, event triggers, scheduling, agent-to-agent coordination, full session traces, and no infra to manage, letting teams plug in any context or compute layer. He closes by urging teams to build their harness, understand the layers, embrace the fast pace of change, and get the execution layer right so everything else can evolve around it.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Dan Farrelly introduces himself as CTO and co-founder of Inngest, building a system that reliably executes agents, workflows, and pipelines. He emphasizes he builds AI infrastructure and agents daily, not just in theory.

sections.title: The 6-month half-life problem
sections.summary: Farrelly notes that anyone building agents for more than six months has likely rewritten something. New models, frameworks, tool-calling standards, and patterns make architectures obsolete. He challenges the audience to consider whether surviving code was designed to survive or survived by accident.

sections.title: Three conceptual layers and their half-lives
sections.summary: He introduces three discrete layers: execution (brain—flow, state, durability, retries), context (knowledge—models, prompts, tools, memory, changes most), and compute (hands—sandboxes, runtimes, browsers). Each has a different half-life: prompts weeks, models months, execution years. Coupling layers causes one short half-life to drag others down. Thesis: think in layers, decouple them.

sections.title: Problems with current approaches
sections.summary: Frameworks, pre-built harnesses, or custom-rolled systems often lack proper abstractions or merge layers—orchestration buried in chains, state kept in sandboxes, retries tangled with prompt logic. Swapping components requires near-total rewrites.

sections.title: Execution layer defined
sections.summary: The execution layer manages the full lifecycle—plan, call models, run code, invoke sub-agents, loop, retry, coordinate—while remaining independent of model, context, or sandbox. Swapping any of those should not require changing the execution layer.

sections.title: Resumability and durable state
sections.summary: Execution must enable resuming after failures without restarting from the beginning. A failed step 38 should retry and continue, not restart. A 3-hour run cannot hold state in memory or disk—state must be durable and external. Manual checkpointing abstractions tend to leak into other layers.

sections.title: Flexible invocation patterns and observability
sections.summary: Execution must support crons, events, APIs, human-in-the-loop, subagents, dynamic workflows, and sync/async/delayed invocation. Without flexible primitives, harness logic absorbs queues, workers, polling, backoff, and scheduling. Full-session observability across triggers, LLM calls, tool calls, database errors, and performance is essential for debugging and improving agents.

sections.title: Sandboxes as anti-pattern for state
sections.summary: Sandboxes are ephemeral and stateless by design; using them for durability, snapshots, or state is an anti-pattern. The execution layer should give the sandbox its context, sequence, and durability. Sandbox is the hands; execution is the brain.

sections.title: Emerging architectures and their demands
sections.summary: Upcoming architectures—background agents, dynamic workflows, autonomous loops, agent factories—are all long-running, asynchronous, and delegated. They must be observable by humans and agents. Background agents may run for minutes or hours with ~200 tool calls and guaranteed failures. Loop architectures run continuously on schedules, assess system state against goals, and delegate to sub-agents.

sections.title: Code example: cron health check and triage agent
sections.summary: Farrelly walks through a code example: a cron runs every 30 minutes, pulls system metrics, passes them to an LLM to assess health. If unhealthy, it invokes a triage agent that pulls detailed context, investigates root cause in a loop, spins up sandboxes, clones code, and analyzes commits. This may run for minutes with uncertain timing, requiring proper execution infrastructure to observe and debug.

sections.title: Reviewer function and the improving loop
sections.summary: A reviewer function runs weekly to evaluate the triage system: is it performing as expected, do prompts need adjustment, does it have the data it needs, is it overreacting? It must be execution-aware and orchestration-aware—pulling logs, understanding what was executed, what sub-agents were fanned out, what workflows were called. It analyzes and either makes changes or reports where performance can improve, completing the improving loop of three functions.

sections.title: Execution layer as hub for observability and scoring
sections.summary: The execution layer sits between user input and system activity, making it the ideal hub for observability. User feedback, actions, and session results all flow through it. To iterate, teams need all this data connected and aware of how code executes. The execution layer is the perfect place to instrument and score agents—deferring scoring tasks after execution with full trace information, inputs, and outputs. Teams can also wait for additional events and attach them to sessions to determine if outcomes were successful.

sections.title: Inngest as the execution layer and wrap-up
sections.summary: Farrelly positions Inngest as durable execution for AI agents—the execution layer where any context or compute layer can be plugged in. It provides durable steps, small primitives, event triggers, scheduling, agent-to-agent coordination, full session traces, and no infra to manage. He closes by urging teams to build their harness, understand the layers, embrace the fast pace of change, and get the execution layer right so everything else can quickly evolve around it.

demonstrations: Code example of a cron-based health check loop: runs every 30 minutes, pulls system metrics, passes to LLM for health assessment, and if unhealthy invokes a triage agent that pulls detailed metrics, investigates root cause, potentially spins up sandboxes and clones code

Three-function architecture: cron health check, triage agent, and weekly reviewer function that evaluates triage system performance, checks if prompts need adjustment, verifies data availability, and determines if the system is overreacting
Deferred scoring during execution: after a step runs, defer a scoring task with full trace information, inputs, and outputs to evaluate agent performance
Outcome-based scoring examples: triage success measured by whether engineering opened a PR; research agent success measured by whether research was saved or produced a good report
